title: Mohnish Pabrai’s Q&A session with Doctors Investing Group
summary: In a podcast for physician investors, Pabrai recounts his path from IT entrepreneur to fund manager, defines value investing as buying no-brainers well below worth within your circle of competence, and explains shameless cloning, 10x10 concentration, and spawners like Amazon. The centerpiece is his Reysas investment in Turkey at 3% of liquidation value with inflation-indexed leases, followed by his views on inflation, bubbles in crypto and meme stocks, PE ratios, the Free Lunch portfolio, and Dakshana's measurable social return on capital.

ideas.idea: Buffett's approach of few, big, infrequent bets was diametrically opposite to how mutual funds operated, so anyone who actually executed it would have a clear advantage.
ideas.detail: He discovered Buffett in 1994 via a Peter Lynch book and the first biographies; mutual funds had 100% annual turnover and dozens or hundreds of positions. He tested the idea with $1 million from selling part of his IT business, grew it past $10 million at about 70% a year by 1999-2000, and started Pabrai Funds in 1999 as a hobby for eight friends with $1 million.

ideas.idea: Value investing is simply buying things for well below what they are worth; you either get it in five minutes or never.
ideas.detail: A rental apartment netting $12,000 a year is worth no more than $100-120k to someone wanting 10% and no more than $60k to someone wanting 20%; stocks are the same, with the added question of how long the market takes to converge on value. Go for no-brainers where the math can be done in your head without a spreadsheet.

ideas.idea: The first question is always whether a business is within your circle of competence; only then can you value it and compare price to worth.
ideas.detail: A Des Moines apartment investor knows a good local deal instantly but may have no edge in London or Florida real estate. If the gap between price and value is large, step in; if negative or minuscule, move on.

ideas.idea: Index investing is a great way to go for almost everyone; venture into individual stocks only if the business is in your circle and you have the time.
ideas.detail: An ER doctor might understand Walmart, Costco or Apple as a customer, but without time to dig in, better not to go there. The S&P 500, Berkshire Hathaway and his Free Lunch portfolio are all valid starting points.

ideas.idea: His standard is a 10x10 portfolio, and one can be plenty diversified with just four stocks.
ideas.detail: For a $100 million fund he wants ten $10 million bets across a few industries and geographies. Munger said at the Daily Journal meeting the Munger family holds Berkshire (about 80%), Costco, Li Lu's fund and some apartments, which Pabrai considers plenty diversified since Berkshire alone contains over 100 businesses.

ideas.idea: Shameless cloning is bowling with bumpers: start from the highest-conviction bets of investors you admire, then apply your own circle-of-competence filter.
ideas.detail: With over 50,000 listed companies, circle of competence removes 90-95% and cloning cuts the rest dramatically while guaranteeing each idea already passed a great mind's filter with real money behind it. He names Munger, Buffett and Bill Ackman as investors to clone.

ideas.idea: Spawners are businesses with DNA to enter new businesses, letting them transcend the maturity and death that capitalism imposes on almost every company.
ideas.detail: Amazon's own-inventory retail never appealed to him (FedEx cannot deliver a package for under $20), but Amazon used it as a platform to throw things at the wall: the Fire phone was quickly buried while AWS was quietly nurtured and now, with advertising and marketplace, is the bulk of its value. Google, by contrast, bought Android, YouTube and DoubleClick rather than spawning internally, and Waymo has not gained traction.

ideas.idea: Amazon will eventually compete with UPS and FedEx because its fleet is already bigger and its entrepreneur-driver cost structure beats unionized workforces.
ideas.detail: On his relocation drive from California to Texas he counted far more Amazon trucks than UPS or FedEx trucks; he calls Amazon an 'apex' spawner.

ideas.idea: Spawning through acquisition works just as well as organic spawning if the company's hit rate is high; Instagram and YouTube were the best acquisitions ever.
ideas.detail: What matters is whether management knows its competence, whether homegrown businesses or nurturing acquisitions, and is good at sniffing out and scaling deals.

ideas.idea: He is useless at macro and ignores inflation forecasts because with a very large margin of safety, 1% or 7% inflation is a rounding error.
ideas.detail: Inflation can be a tailwind: an owner of already-built apartments collects inflation-adjusted rents on yesterday's capex while fixed-rate loans shrink, so the lender gets hurt, though a future buyer of apartments faces headwinds.

ideas.idea: In 2019 he bought about 35% of Reysas, Turkey's largest warehouse operator, for $7 million at a $20 million market cap, roughly 3% of an $800 million-plus liquidation value.
ideas.detail: Reysas had 12 million square feet across 82 warehouses, 99% leased on long inflation-indexed leases to tenants like Amazon, Ikea and Carrefour; at $60-80 per square foot replacement cost the real estate was worth about $840 million against $200 million of debt. Other assets, the largest freight rail network, truck fleet, forklift rental and vehicle inspection stations, were monopoly-like and carried no debt. The math took ten minutes with no calculator once he had eliminated fraud risk by visiting warehouses and meeting the father-son team.

ideas.idea: A fully built asset base with inflation-indexed rents cannot lose value in high inflation, which is why he invested knowing Turkish inflation would run 50% a year.
ideas.detail: From 2019 to 2022 Reysas cut debt from $200 million to $90 million at a 14% blended rate while receiving 20-25% CPI rent increases; leases reset to market only every 10 years, only 15-20% of the footprint is at market rent, and a spawned solar business added about $200 million of intrinsic value. Despite the lira falling from 5 to nearly 14 per dollar, dollar intrinsic value is higher than in 2019 and the market cap is over $100 million yet still deeply undervalued.

ideas.idea: In Turkey he limits himself to businesses with lira costs and euro or dollar revenues, where devaluation is a tailwind rather than a risk.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: A Turkish packaged-juice exporter sends 98% of output duty-free to Europe with lira costs and euro revenue, so its input costs fall as the lira depreciates. Every professional investor has exited Turkey over its fiscal policies, and mass exodus creates mass mispricing; he is 'buying every day'.

ideas.idea: Do not be jaundiced about where a company is based; look for great managements, protected monopoly-like products and high returns on capital, then overlay the country.
ideas.detail: He would not sell a single Reysas share at a $1 billion market cap because the young, gifted son and father are excellent capital allocators who could make it worth $5-15 billion in 10-20 years; he might consider selling at $1.5-2 billion.

ideas.idea: Auction-driven markets swing between extreme greed and extreme fear, and that fluctuation, not private negotiation, is what makes value investing possible.
ideas.detail: Reysas could sell one or two of its 82 warehouses to private buyers for $70-80 million each and retire all its debt, yet the whole company traded at $20 million; a stock's 52-week range might be 50 to 120 while a house moves under 5% a year. If he had to negotiate directly, the owners would say it is not for sale below a billion.

ideas.idea: The US market is not in a bubble overall, but crypto and 10-15 meme stocks like AMC and GameStop are, and bargains of 50-70% off are few and far between.
ideas.detail: It is not clear to him that Tesla, Google or Apple are overvalued given strong businesses and low rates, but they are not bargains either; he does not short bubbles and spends more time in places like Turkey where rationality has gone out the window.

ideas.idea: PE ratios are not very useful: a 4x company can be overvalued and an 80x company undervalued; value is future cash over 5-15 years discounted back.
ideas.detail: A melting ice cube with earnings falling 50% a year may not be worth one times earnings, while a business growing 40% a year with long tailwinds can deserve a 100 multiple. Investors should look for no-brainers where no DCF is needed.

ideas.idea: A 3% of liquidation value opportunity has appeared once in 28-30 years, but one such bet at 10% of the portfolio can carry everything else.
ideas.detail: If Reysas becomes a $3-5 billion business in 10-20 years, the $7 million becomes a hundred-bagger and it will not matter how wise or stupid the other bets were.

ideas.idea: He found his Turkish ideas by cloning a local value-fund manager who had already filtered the market, spending a week visiting every company in that portfolio.
ideas.detail: The friend, a Graham-trained investor who attended Pabrai's 2014 meeting, gave decades of history on the families behind each business. 'Bowling with bumpers in Istanbul is awesome.'

ideas.idea: The Free Lunch portfolio is a free, fee-less 15-stock quasi-index built from cloned ideas, spawners and cannibals, rebalanced only once a year.
ideas.detail: It is not a stock-picking or money-making product for him; low activity lets the businesses run, and it does reasonably well.

ideas.idea: Large inheritances are a disservice to your gene pool, so the only choice is to give the money back to society, and to do it thoughtfully while you still have energy.
ideas.detail: Around 2006-07 at age 42 he saw his wealth would exceed his ability to spend it and followed Buffett's line about giving kids enough to do anything but not enough to do nothing; he did not want to be writing Red Cross checks at 85 'drooling with half my brain gone'.

ideas.idea: Most charities are all heart and no head; philanthropy needs a Bill Gates-style balance and a focus on social return on invested capital.
ideas.detail: Comparing housing a homeless person versus needle exchanges versus climate change is nearly impossible to measure, so following Munger's 'invert, always invert' he chose to fund only causes where measurement is easy, which led to education and poverty alleviation in India.

ideas.idea: Dakshana lifts a family permanently out of poverty for about $3,000 by coaching poor, gifted students into nearly free government engineering and medical schools.
ideas.detail: Two years of free coaching yields a 70-80% admission rate; students from families earning under $100-200 a month go on to earn $1,000-2,000 a month. Results are verified by third parties and published at dakshana.org, and Buffett has called the Dakshana annual reports the best nonprofit reports he has ever read.
